solver_side: the CPU reference solver, the cost of producing a new solution today; the GPU-native solver of section 8.5 is 71.7-171.5x faster and shifts the speed-up column down by about two orders of magnitude without touching accuracy
metric: combined relative L2 over both displacement components, ||e||/||u||, every row scored against the SAME N=101 reference -- the convergence-study convention of section 4.4, not the per-component average of Tables 5, 11 and 12

shape.note: the operator error falls at every refinement, from 8.87% at N=13 to 3.72% at N=49, with no minimum inside the range. That is the same shape Table 12 found for this material and material only: B1 x Mooney-Rivlin is the one case of the three whose zero-shot error keeps improving to the finest mesh tested. B1 x Neo-Hookean in Table 18 instead bottoms out at N=37 (3.69%) and worsens after.

reading.the_two_methods_do_not_compete_on_accura: the finite-element solver at its coarsest setting -- N=13, 169 nodes, 20.4 s -- reaches 0.624%, already 14.2x more accurate than the operator at its best (3.72% at N=49). There is no mesh in this sweep at which the operator matches even the cheapest finite-element solve, exactly as for B1 x Neo-Hookean.
reading.the_case_rests_on_how_cost_scales: operator inference is flat in mesh size -- 5.512 to 5.814 ms from 169 to 2,401 nodes, a fourteenfold increase in problem size for a 5% increase in cost -- while the finite-element solve grows superlinearly, so the speed-up climbs from 3,574x to 56,353x across the sweep.
reading.against_Table_18: B1 x Neo-Hookean spans 1,630x to 25,676x on the same nine meshes. Mooney-Rivlin's speed-ups are about 2.2x larger throughout because its CPU assembly costs 2.1-2.4x more (Table 4a, autodiff tangent) while the operator's forward pass is material-independent -- 5.5 ms here against 5.5 ms there, the same architecture on the same meshes.

cost: A100. The run manifest recorded 14 h 31 m for this case. The notebook cell predicted 'roughly two hours, possibly more', which was wrong by about sevenfold -- the estimate was carried over from the B1 x Neo-Hookean run without allowing for Mooney-Rivlin's 2.1-2.4x more expensive CPU assembly, and the sweep spends nearly all its time in 20 CPU solves at each of nine resolutions, the largest of which is 5.5 minutes each.
